items.prompt: Sort 10 million exam scores, each an integer from 0 to 100.
items.why: A small key range → counting sort in O(n + k), beating any comparison sort.

items.prompt: Given non-negative integers, arrange them so that their concatenation is the largest possible number.
items.why: The order is decided pairwise (which of two numbers should come first in the concatenation?) → sort with a custom comparator, then join.

items.prompt: Return the k-th largest element of an unsorted array of 10^6 numbers, with k = 10.
items.why: Only the top k matter → a size-k min-heap, O(n log k), or quickselect. Sorting everything is wasted work.

items.prompt: Find the minimum absolute difference between any two elements of an array.
items.why: After sorting, the closest pair is adjacent → sort, then one linear scan of neighbours.
Sorting by start is only step one; the overlap sweep that extends or closes the current interval is the Merge Intervals pattern.

items.prompt: Sort an array that contains only 0s, 1s and 2s, in one pass and in place.
items.why: Dutch national flag: low / mid / high pointers swap each element into its zone in one pass. A general sort is O(n log n).

items.prompt: Combine k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
items.why: The inputs are already sorted → keep a heap of the k list heads, O(N log k). Re-sorting everything ignores that order.

items.prompt: A researcher's h-index is the largest h such that h papers have at least h citations each. Compute it from the citation counts.
items.why: Sort descending and find the last position i with citations[i] ≥ i + 1. Or counting-sort the capped counts for O(n).

items.prompt: Every element of an array is at most k positions away from its sorted position. Sort it efficiently.
items.why: Only the next k + 1 elements can hold the minimum → a size-(k+1) min-heap gives O(n log k). Insertion sort's O(n·k) is the simpler fallback.
